tGFZOrwzK8c.title: Our Communal Covenant: Your End of the Bargain - Presence
tGFZOrwzK8c.one_line: The first thing the community owes its masjid is presence: showing up consistently is an underrated superpower through which people learn, understand, improve, connect and belong.
tGFZOrwzK8c.summary: He opens with the first warm day after a long winter as a sign that Allah's sun always returns if you hold your ground, and contrasts it with humanity's darkest winter: elected criminals bombing the land where Imam Muslim was born while the ummah debates whether it may even pray for the victims. Reading history, especially the Mongol devastation, convinces him Muslims will rise again. Having restated the masjid's ten commitments last week, he begins the community's side with presence. Only one Muslim in thousands will ever speak from a minbar; most of the work is simply showing up, which needs no funding or permission. He cites Bowlby's attachment research on one reliable person, notes that Bill C-9 passes because Muslims are absent from the tables where laws and curricula are decided, and argues that attendance at London's first mosque in the 1960s was ninety percent of the community while today it is two or three. The Prophet's weight on attendance appears in the hadith of the seven in Allah's shade and in Ibn Mas'ud's report that only known hypocrites missed the congregation. Showing up brings five things: you learn, you understand others, you correct yourselves, you network and you belong. He asks for three days a week, with children. The second khutbah reads Surah At-Tawbah as repentance for failing to show up at Tabuk.

outline.heading: Opening
The sun always shines again
outline.gist: A warm day after months of winter is Allah's reminder that the sun returns if you hold your ground. Go out today and praise Him for what He made.

outline.heading: Humanity's darkest winter is unnecessary
outline.gist: Past winters came from ignorance and lack of guidance; today's brutality is known to everyone. Leaders people voted in keep bombing countries they dislike while the ummah argues over whether it may make dua for the victims.

outline.heading: The Mongols: there have been worse times
outline.gist: Reading how the Mongols wiped out the eastern caliphate and how Muslims rose again is what keeps him going; we can rise again, more efficiently than before.

outline.heading: The covenant must run both ways
outline.gist: Last week he restated the ten points he and his team committed to when the centre opened: a welcoming, open masjid with programming and pure content. Now he asks what the community commits to.

outline.heading: Bombing the land of Imam Muslim
outline.gist: If you do not want to sit watching television while they bomb the region where Islam's scholars came from, the country Imam Muslim was born in, you must commit to your side.

outline.heading: Human rights only when others break them
outline.gist: This is not empires colliding but decency, justice and equality, words applied only to others. Speaking out threatens your job and credibility, and when people like him die it is just a statistic.

outline.heading: Every life matters
outline.gist: No child should die in its sleep under the rubble of its home; that is our faith, even though others do not hold the same principles.

outline.heading: Presence, the underrated superpower
outline.gist: Only one Muslim in thousands will ever speak from a minbar, and 99 percent of the work is beyond it. Most of it is simply showing up, which needs only intention, empathy and care; thriving teams are people who kept showing up.

outline.heading: One reliable person: Bowlby on attachment
outline.gist: A child needs only one reliable person who shows up every day to be resilient; imagine a whole community that is always present. You do not have to be perfect, just there, and when you are absent you lose touch with people's struggles.

outline.heading: Absent from the tables: Bill C-9
outline.gist: When you are absent your heart stops caring. Muslims are missing from the tables where laws and curricula are decided, which is why Bill C-9 goes through; we are more present in the country than in our masajid.

outline.heading: Percentages, not numbers: London's first mosque
outline.gist: When the London Muslim Mosque opened in the 1960s its small congregation was 90 percent of the community. A thousand times more people at two or three percent is going backwards.

outline.heading: Seven in Allah's shade: the heart attached to the masjid
outline.gist: The hadith names the one whose heart is attached to the masjid and the youth raised in Allah's obedience. A young person grows up that way only by being in the masjid.

outline.heading: Ibn Mas'ud: only the known hypocrite stayed away
outline.gist: Only a man known for his hypocrisy missed the congregation, and the sick were carried between two men to stand in the line.

outline.heading: Showing up takes courage
outline.gist: No one can attend every prayer, but without presence nothing gets fixed. It takes courage to keep coming when you are tired, uncomfortable or standing beside people you disagree with.

outline.heading: Umar's turn-taking with a friend
outline.gist: The Prophet knew his people because they showed up daily, and those who could not sent someone. Work kept Umar from attending every day, so he and a friend alternated and briefed each other.

outline.heading: Faces that come and go
outline.gist: Presence must be consistent for years. Since age five he has watched enthusiastic faces come for a year or two and vanish, and a population never becomes a community that way.

outline.heading: Benefit 1: you learn
outline.gist: If people attended, he would not field thousands of questions about Good Friday that he has answered many times, or be texted like an on-call sheikh.

outline.heading: The Muslim view of Isa
outline.gist: We love Isa, honour his miraculous birth and await his return, but he was not on the cross. That difference does not stop us living with Christians and respecting their beliefs.

outline.heading: Nobody delivers Islam to your door
outline.gist: Fathers must bring their sons and mothers their daughters; no sheikh comes by Amazon. Every dictator in the Middle East hates masajid and bombs them first.

outline.heading: Number seventeen on the list of those who prayed
outline.gist: In Syria his name was on an intelligence list of people who prayed, which he values above his medical degree, because masajid are where change happens and consistent attendance moves the needle.

outline.heading: Benefit 2: you understand others
outline.gist: Attending pulls you out of the bubble of family and friends into other Muslims' struggles. He was baffled by masjid board members who never came; at this centre anyone on the board must be present daily with ears on the ground.

outline.heading: Benefit 3: you correct yourselves
outline.gist: The most important for Muslims in the West: when people see each other, wrong behaviour is seen and right behaviour spreads, so the community slowly improves.

outline.heading: Benefit 4: you network
outline.gist: Showing up builds friendships and ends loneliness. A community must know each other by name, which cannot happen if you only come for Jumuah or Eid.

outline.heading: Benefit 5: you belong
outline.gist: Children stay Muslim only if they belong, so bring them consistently. Start with three days a week, or at least once beyond Jumuah; leaving because you dislike how masajid run fixes nothing.

outline.heading: Interlude
Surah At-Tawbah: repentance for not being there
outline.gist: The verses he opened with are from the surah of Tabuk, whose repentance was for staying behind when the Prophet went out. Those who fled at Uhud were pardoned because they had at least shown up.

outline.heading: Even the weak came to give their excuse
outline.gist: The sick, elderly and poor without mounts or weapons were not blamed, but they still came to offer their excuse, advice and dua.

outline.heading: Hearts sealed for those who stayed behind
outline.gist: The able who chose to stay back had their hearts sealed. Showing up for each other, for the deen and for Allah is a superpower that moves the needle.

outline.heading: Outro

jKJ9INEVe-c.summary: He opens by explaining his method. A surah is a fenced-in unit with one message. The last part of the Quran is a cheat sheet of the whole deen, organized in clusters, and Muslims who recite these short surahs daily should know what each teaches so they can reflect and turn to the right passage in hardship. After recapping the surah's three proofs, he adds that life itself is driven to survive, a programming that needs a programmer. Verses 35-40 describe a Day when the deniers can speak but have no permission to apologize, when life on earth feels like a day or less, and when all humanity is gathered and dared to plot. He ties that dare to humanity's present arrogance: environmental collapse, weapons races, racism and voting morally empty leaders into power. The pious receive true shade, springs and fruit, told to eat without guilt. Bowing (ruku) is explained as taking the knee: Islam replaced kneeling to kings with the bay'ah, a pledge between equals, and Muslims kneel to no one but Allah. The last verse asks in what narrative they will believe if not this, so Muslims must represent and live Islam.

outline.heading: Clusters as a compass for reflection
outline.gist: Surahs come in clusters around a shared theme, each addressing it from its own angle. Knowing that theme is the compass that keeps you from contemplating in the middle of the ocean.

outline.heading: A surah is a fenced-in unit
outline.gist: The mufassal, as the Prophet named the final section, is rich in surahs. Surah shares a root with siwar, a bracelet, and sur, a fence: however short, it encloses its own message, so Al-Baqarah and the shortest surah are equal as units.

outline.heading: The last four juz are the cheat sheets
outline.gist: A book ends with a summary that puts everything in perspective. If you cannot memorize much, know these surahs: they hold the basics of Islam, which is why children start from the end.

outline.heading: First cluster: choices
outline.gist: Each surah of the first cluster offers a choice: righteousness or falsehood, purpose or aimlessness, guidance or misguidance, knowledge or ignorance.

outline.heading: Second cluster: organizing society
outline.gist: Juz 28 is entirely Medinan and sets out relationships among Muslims, with the state, with non-Muslim neighbours, with religious leadership and with those who are dead weight.

outline.heading: Third cluster: what representing Islam requires
outline.gist: Spreading the message by word or by action needs a measure of knowledge, ethics, spirituality and conduct; without all four it crumbles.

outline.heading: Two examples of dawah
outline.gist: One caller gave every effort and did not see the outcome, another succeeded without knowing it: you control only your effort.

outline.heading: Inner fuel, outward conduct and three appeals
outline.gist: Al-Muzzammil supplies the inner fuel and Al-Muddaththir how you carry yourself; then three surahs appeal to the intellect, to reward and to just punishment. The fourth cluster comes next.

outline.heading: Interlude
Know what the surahs you recite are saying
outline.gist: Many recite Al-Buruj daily with no idea what it teaches. Keep reciting the short surahs, but understand them so that you contemplate as you read.

outline.heading: You cannot reflect on words you do not understand
outline.gist: Words that roll off the tongue while the mind is elsewhere bring little benefit. Since we lack the original command of Arabic, the teacher has to supply what the first hearers grasped.

outline.heading: The first hearers understood and chose to deny
outline.gist: The theme of each surah was effortlessly clear to Abu Jahl and the Meccan polytheists; they knew exactly what each unit taught and rejected it.

outline.heading: A book with no point gets thrown away
outline.gist: Many enjoy a reciter's voice but cannot tell where a surah is going, even with a translation, like a novel whose plot never appears. Every surah has a thread sewn through its verses, or it would not be a surah.

outline.heading: Knowing what you are learning from each surah
outline.gist: Hearing Al-Mursalat, you know Allah is calling you through reverence; hearing Nuh, you learn from perfect dawah that did not get the outcome. Every surah works this way.

outline.heading: Interlude
Short surahs as pills that hold the whole deen
outline.gist: Millions recite these surahs every night, but what is each one saying and what did the Prophet carry from it? If the mufassal summarizes the Quran, these short surahs condense every value, principle and behaviour like small pills.

outline.heading: Interlude
The themes were obvious to the first Arabs
outline.gist: Help others grasp what An-Naba or An-Nazi'at is about. The early Arabs never discussed the themes because they were as obvious as breathing; a scholar of that era would find this lesson redundant, but it was not clear to him growing up, so he studied it.

outline.heading: A teacher who never went to school
outline.gist: One of his teachers, never schooled, speaks flawless classical Arabic and finds the surahs' points self-evident. That is why he teaches each surah's purpose rather than word roots or stories you can look up, so the lesson can be internalized.

outline.heading: Turn to the surah that speaks to your state
outline.gist: When his heart grows rusty a passage humbles him, and when gratitude is hard the right surahs restore it. Who else do you turn to when lost and afraid? Reading At-Tawbah's rules on foreign relations when you are broke is the wrong chapter for your problem.

outline.heading: Why the Quran came in pieces
outline.gist: It was revealed piece by piece to strengthen the Prophet, each part tackling a problem he faced, so later believers can apply the same verses to theirs and find clarity, safety or ease.

outline.heading: Interlude
Recap: everything leaves an impact, and the Day of distinction
outline.gist: Everything is sent with good or harm, spreads it, makes a difference and leaves a legacy; just as that is real, the promised Day is real, when truth is no longer lost among waves of falsehood.

outline.heading: Recap: what takdhib means
outline.gist: Takdhib is refusing what you see as correct because it is unpopular or would mean eating your words, for the sake of status, money or ego. It starts with sins and ends with denying Allah.

outline.heading: Recap: the lesson of history
outline.gist: The first of three simple arguments: dictators, the powerful and the oppressive fall and their legacies vanish everywhere, while whatever is good remains.

outline.heading: Life is driven to survive: who wrote the programming?
outline.gist: A new point on the second argument: biologically, life is purposeful. Every living thing wants to keep living, reproduce and adapt; where did a first cell, supposedly a coincidence in volcanic water, get that drive?

outline.heading: A child's will to live outgrows you
outline.gist: Once a baby takes its first breath it becomes a force of life its parents cannot control; the harder you try, the worse it gets, so let life live.

outline.heading: No biology degree needed: someone put it there
outline.gist: The Quran asks only for basic contemplation. The only answer to where life's programming came from is that someone placed it; we are here as the lineage of those who survived and adapted.

outline.heading: The world, and the odds against your existence
outline.gist: Earth's features are set so precisely that any small change would end life as we know it. Each person is a miracle: one sperm among hundreds of millions, a DNA that will never recur, odds beyond what calculators can show.

outline.heading: Recap: the shade and the sparks
outline.gist: The deniers are sent to what they denied, a three-branched shade with no coolness or protection, and sparks as big as palaces like a caravan of yellow camels.

outline.heading: A Day they will not speak
outline.gist: He recites the closing passage. On this Day they cannot articulate a word and are given no permission to offer their excuses.

outline.heading: Able to speak, but without permission
outline.gist: The rules change: basic functions that are free today, like speaking or sitting, need permission, as for someone held captive.

outline.heading: Eager to apologize, but the books are closed
outline.gist: They plead to be sent back to do better and want to admit their wrong and seek forgiveness, but are not allowed. Most painful of all, Allah will not speak to them, look at them or purify them.

outline.heading: How long did we stay? Time blurs
outline.gist: Whispering, they ask how long they lived. Memory fades: by forty a whole year can vanish, by seventy decades. They honestly answer a day or part of one, and tell Allah to ask those who keep count.

outline.heading: You stayed only a little, if only you had known
outline.gist: Allah confirms the time was short; the regret is not having grasped in life how short, finite and fragile it was.

outline.heading: Save the apology for now: repentance is open today
outline.gist: Hardship destroys the sense of time. On that Day everything is clear and the apology is refused, but an apology to Allah right now, even without words, is accepted, and no one who turns back is rejected.

outline.heading: The Day of sorting: Adam's right and left
outline.gist: On the Night Journey the Prophet saw Adam before a vast mass of his descendants, smiling at those on his right and weeping at those on his left: those who chose well and those who did not.

outline.heading: Only Allah knows who is where
outline.gist: In this life we go by outward appearances; who ends up on which side is Allah's decision alone. All we can hope is to meet Him having never refused a truth that was clear to us.

outline.heading: Gathered with all before you: if you have a plot, use it
outline.gist: All humanity is gathered together. The noon of fa-kidun carries a kasra because the ya of the original kiduni is dropped, and the reciter stops on it.

outline.heading: A dare from God
outline.gist: You built AI; go ahead and plot your way out. This is no comic-book defiance: the verse is a declaration from Allah, and there will be nothing to offer.

outline.heading: If we still do not see our weakness, nothing will teach us
outline.gist: Environmental collapse, the race for weapons that could destroy the planet, racial profiling and driving people from their land: humanity has not learned how fragile it is or that we are not enemies.

outline.heading: We keep electing the morally empty
outline.gist: People hand power to leaders who care only for themselves, in systems rigged to cap ordinary people. This was always known: an ordinary Arab man in 1955 could tell you the same.

outline.heading: The last word on punishment: nothing to offer
outline.gist: This is nearly the last verse on punishment: everyone is gathered and dared, and humanity can do nothing but run to the prophets asking them to intercede.

outline.heading: The pious in true shade, springs and fruit
outline.gist: Against Hell's false shade, the mindful are in true shade among springs, with whatever fruit they desire.

outline.heading: Eat and drink without guilt
outline.gist: They are told to enjoy themselves for what they did. No one enters Paradise by deeds alone, yet Allah frames it that way so they never feel like impostors; so He rewards those who excel.

outline.heading: Woe: how could they deny every daily miracle?
outline.gist: While their counterparts enjoy Paradise, how could the deniers look at the sun, moon, mountains, rivers and life itself every day and say it means nothing?

outline.heading: Back to this life: enjoy a little, you criminals
outline.gist: The scene of the Day ends and the verses return to the living: eat and enjoy briefly, you who break not human law but Allah's.

outline.heading: Ruku as taking the knee
outline.gist: When told to bow, they would not. Bowing historically meant taking the knee in a king's court: I am not your peer but your servant. Leaders still look for who will take the knee to them.

outline.heading: Bay'ah instead of kneeling
outline.gist: Islam replaced taking the knee with the bay'ah: you stand on both legs and pledge, the leader serves you, and you hold him accountable while he obeys Allah.

outline.heading: Muslims kneel to no one but Allah
outline.gist: Muslims later turned rule into monarchy, but the bay'ah made it hard to sustain. We do not kneel even to our own leaders; we offer a covenant of common good, and royal bloodlines are nonsense.

outline.heading: Bowing marks the Creator from the creation
outline.gist: Bowing to the One who made you establishes the difference: you are created, flawed, weak and finite and He is none of these. Some dislike this deep down, yet will take the knee to a person for wealth or status.

outline.heading: In what narrative after this will they believe?
outline.gist: The verse closes not just the surah but the whole cluster. Hadith means a whole way of life; if this does not convince, nothing will, so Muslims must represent and live Islam so others see its truth.

outline.heading: Outro

38:22.ar: إِذۡ دَخَلُواْ عَلَىٰ دَاوُۥدَ فَفَزِعَ مِنۡهُمۡۖ قَالُواْ لَا تَخَفۡۖ خَصۡمَانِ بَغَىٰ بَعۡضُنَا عَلَىٰ بَعۡضࣲ فَٱحۡكُم بَيۡنَنَا بِٱلۡحَقِّ وَلَا تُشۡطِطۡ وَٱهۡدِنَآ إِلَىٰ سَوَآءِ ٱلصِّرَٰطِ

zWbSaJC7aHk.title: Tafseer of Surat Al-Mursalat, Part 2: Verses 16-34
zWbSaJC7aHk.one_line: Al-Mursalat's three proofs for eman (history, the creation of life, the earth), Hell's shade and sparks, and why refusing known truth is the gravest ethical breach.
zWbSaJC7aHk.summary: He first explains the surah's refrain, woe to the deniers. Kufr is a neutral description and a scholarly term laypeople should not throw around, while takdhib is refusing a truth you have recognized, out of ego, tribe or fear. That is the first ethic of a Muslim, which is why the surah hammers it. Prophets in Surat Sad returned when corrected; Iblis dug in. Verses 16-28 then give three sources of eman. History shows that those who break moral law fall fast and vanish, as the Syrian regime he grew up under did, and as Persia, Rome and later the Mongol-struck caliphate did. Life shows a code no one wrote by accident: understanding the recipe does not mean nobody cooked it. The earth is set up so we can live on it. He argues eman must rest on these constants, not on variables like an answered dua or a good year, which is why the final message came without a physical miracle. Verses 29-33 describe the deniers sent toward a three-branched shade of Hell's smoke that gives no cool and sparks like palaces or yellow camels. He closes by urging the young to follow truth before loyalties make them bend it, and to teach children not to lie.

outline.heading: Opening
The last juz: the summary of the summary
outline.gist: Every Muslim should try to memorize the final part of the Quran: it repeats in short surahs the conclusions of the first 26 years of revelation, which is why children learn it first. It holds the core values, ethics and concepts of Islam, the summary of the summary.

outline.heading: Al-Mursalat: dawah through warning, held together by its refrain
outline.gist: In the cluster on representing Islam, Al-Qiyamah calls through the intellect, Al-Insan through reward and Al-Mursalat through warning. Its key is the refrain repeated between paragraphs, without which the surah stays unclear.

outline.heading: Kafir is a description, not an insult
outline.gist: Kufr is a general term for the line between Muslim and non-Muslim; he is a kafir to Christians as they are to him. Never say it of a Muslim: whoever calls his brother a kafir, one of the two carries it.

outline.heading: Leave scholarly terms to scholars
outline.gist: Some words belong to specialists, as medical terms do. His worst clinical encounters are patients who parrot words from Google or ChatGPT; acting as if you know what you do not is unhealthy, and he himself knows very little.

outline.heading: A kafir's situation is unknown; a mukadhdhib saw the truth
outline.gist: The refrain requires knowing the truth. A kafir may never have met a Muslim, as in a remote village in India, or lived between prophets where religion never reached; takdhib is when the truth was presented, assessed and refused.

outline.heading: Whatever the reason, refusing truth and Islam do not mix
outline.gist: Ego, pride, fear or dislike of the one making the argument make no difference. Unconditional acceptance of a correct argument, about anything, is the hallmark of a Muslim, and it is liberating to have no agenda to defend.

outline.heading: Abu Jahl: I know he is truthful
outline.gist: Abu Jahl admitted to a younger man of Quraysh that Muhammad told the truth, but his clan and Banu Hashim had raced each other like two horses for honour, and he could not concede them a prophet. Someone who honestly found it unconvincing is a different case.

outline.heading: Takdhib breaches the first ethic
outline.gist: Presented properly, most reasonable people accept the truth. Kufr carries much ambiguity, but takdhib is where the punishment lies, because refusing the truth breaches the first ethic, after which nothing else matters.

outline.heading: Prophets who returned when corrected
outline.gist: Surat Sad gives examples: Dawud judged before hearing the other party and repented once it was clear, Sulayman was distracted by the horses from prayer, and Ayyub swore an oath about his wife and was given a way out.

outline.heading: Iblis dug in his heels
outline.gist: Iblis was given a way out and refused it. When caught in a mistake you choose to return to the truth or dig in; some get away with it in court, but the ethical breach haunts you until you admit it.

outline.heading: The refrain as a hammer: seek the truth and you are safe
outline.gist: Allah repeats the refrain until you resolve never to refuse the truth. Always asking what is right, with nothing to defend even when ego, reputation or family creep in, keeps you safe for life. He then recites verses 16-19, the first of three arguments for accepting Allah.

outline.heading: First source of eman: history
outline.gist: After a recitation note, verses 16-17: Allah destroyed the earlier nations and made the later ones follow. To arrive in the world with no interest in what happened before you makes no sense.

outline.heading: Those who break the moral law fall and vanish
outline.gist: Once you look, a pattern repeats everywhere: empires, kings and dictators who break the moral and ethical laws meet a horrible end and disappear so completely that little is left of them. So Allah deals with the criminals.

outline.heading: The regime he grew up under
outline.gist: He lived on land owned by others, with no rights and no voice, and never thought its rulers would leave. How fast and completely they vanished is a lesson he will teach his children: do not be taken in by worldly power.

outline.heading: What lasts, and why strength is not ours
outline.gist: Only those who uphold their morals and seek the truth leave a legacy that outlives them. Repeated falls show that true strength is not something humans possess or can sustain.

outline.heading: Persia flattened within a decade
outline.gist: The Persian Empire, vast in numbers, wealth and resources, fell in less than ten years to the Arabs who read these verses, a freckle on the face of the peninsula.

outline.heading: Rome, the Mongols, and the pattern denied
outline.gist: Rome fell just as fast. When Muslims grew careless and let corruption in, the Mongols swept Khurasan, Bukhara and Baghdad until they were pushed back in Egypt and later accepted Islam. Woe to those who see this pattern of what lasts and what vanishes and deny it.

outline.heading: Two accepted ways to recite alam nakhluqkum
outline.gist: The qaf can merge fully into the kaf, the more widespread choice, or keep a trace of itself; he uses the second so newcomers do not think a letter was dropped. Both are correct.

outline.heading: The nasal sound in the refrain
outline.gist: Since the refrain recurs so often, recite it properly: the tanween merges into the lam of lil-mukadhdhibin with no nasal trace, while the one before the ya carries it through the nose.

outline.heading: Second source: life from an undistinguished fluid
outline.gist: Did We not create you from ma' mahin, a fluid with no honour that neither gushes from a spring nor falls from the sky, and place it in a firm, protected lodging?

outline.heading: The womb, the most impressive organ
outline.gist: The womb's ability to contract and expand as it does has no parallel; without a vessel that strong and protected, life could never have existed.

outline.heading: An appointed term, set by the best of planners
outline.gist: The fluid stays for a known measure of time, and Allah praises His own planning: the process happens exactly as it needs to.

outline.heading: Embryology: cells that know what to become
outline.gist: Two strands of DNA meet and divide; some cells become the placenta that is discarded and others the person, then eyes, ears and spine, and no one knows why. If ChatGPT impresses you, look at this code.

outline.heading: Figuring out the recipe does not mean no one cooked it
outline.gist: Science will explain more of how it happens, but understanding the coding does not mean no one coded it. Human arrogance mistakes figuring out a puzzle for having made it.

outline.heading: Look in the mirror
outline.gist: We can only manipulate what already has a code. Your thought, emotion, hope and love came from a humble fluid left for nine months, and ten years later that child argues back with you; Allah is the best of planners.

outline.heading: Third source: an earth that gathers the living and the dead
outline.gist: Kifat means a place that gathers things together: the earth holds the living and the lifeless, with high mountains and fresh water to drink. You need no astronomy for eman; look at what surrounds you.

outline.heading: Everything set up for you, and the refrain intensifies
outline.gist: Whatever you need when hungry, thirsty, cold or afraid is there. After each proof the refrain grows more intense: why refuse to deduce anything from all this?

outline.heading: Build eman on constants, not variables
outline.gist: Eman built on an answered dua, provision or a success becomes a variable and weakens when they go, yet eman is meant to lift you when things turn sour.

outline.heading: The final message left constants, not shows of miracles
outline.gist: Musa offered the staff and the hand again and again, but those are variables. The Prophet had signs yet never used them as a challenge; he left thought, principle and a way of seeing the world to build on.

outline.heading: History again: the same story in every civilization
outline.gist: Every people received a messenger. Civilizations that could not communicate share the same outline of a man, a woman and a serpent, and many lacked schools or bathrooms but every one had a temple.

outline.heading: Life again: a maker with at least what He made
outline.gist: Intelligence and metacognition that bend the environment come from the code of a double helix. Someone made this, and whoever made beings who think, see and will must have at least those attributes.

outline.heading: The earth again: a planet tuned for us
outline.gist: Everything is set so we can live; a degree of warming from melting ice caps and released methane would end us, which shows whoever set it up meant for you to be here.

outline.heading: Reciting verses 29-34: the tha letters
outline.gist: He recites the description of the deniers' fate. The verse with dhi thalathi is ideal practice for the letters made by pushing the tongue through the teeth.

outline.heading: Go forth to what you used to deny
outline.gist: Those who refused the truths of history, life and the world are told intaliqu: begin a long journey of stations toward the very thing they called myth and control, though they knew better.

outline.heading: Hell kindled until it turned black
outline.gist: He describes the fire through the narration that it was kindled a thousand years until red, a thousand until white and a thousand until black.

outline.heading: A shade of three branches
outline.gist: The fire is so dense it casts a shade, and flames rise in branches. Some say the three are fire, smoke and heat; scholars admit they do not know and hope never to find out.

outline.heading: Neither cool nor shield from the flame
outline.gist: Zalil is the cooling shade the desert Arabs longed for; this shade gives no coolness and no protection, under a sun drawn close.

outline.heading: Sparks like palaces and yellow camels
outline.gist: A spark, like those from a cheap lighter, here is as large as a palace and looks like a caravan of yellow camels. Shade and spark sound harmless, which makes the image all the more terrible.

outline.heading: Read it all week: a recap of the surah
outline.gist: Woe that day to the deniers. Read the surah daily and feel the refrain intensify: everything leaves an impact, the promise is as real, the cosmos will collapse, the prophets will come to their appointment, all leading to woe for those who refuse truth.

outline.heading: Follow the truth before you are invested
outline.gist: His advice to the young: with no cause, group, country or project yet to defend, you can simply follow what is right. Once invested, you start making things look better than they are.

outline.heading: Lying is breaking the truth
outline.gist: Turning from the truth once makes it easier, which is why children must be taught never to lie, even when the truth is a headache. Small lies grow until the truth means nothing, and clever people end up arguing it cannot be defined, though everyone knows what is right.

outline.heading: Truth-tellers are attacked, and the truth must be respected
outline.gist: Prophets were killed for saying the truth because it is painful to hear. The companions fought because they did what they judged true at all costs; the safer, quieter path is no substitute.

ALPiW4_TFT4.speaker_note: MWN Friday khutbah, third in his own 'Communal Covenant' series; refers to his 13 years in the city and his 2022 khutbah on champions
ALPiW4_TFT4.title: Our Communal Covenant: Your End of the Bargain - Initiative
ALPiW4_TFT4.one_line: The third communal commitment: take initiative and fill the voids nobody is filling, because every void is filled with good or evil and there is no third option.
ALPiW4_TFT4.summary: Opening with 2:148, race to good deeds, he restates the covenant frame: the masjid has said what it owes, the community owes attendance and participation, and now initiative. In 13 years he has heard endless ideas but seen few initiatives, and the excuse of a dictatorship he once accepted in Syria does not apply here. An initiative means noticing a need nobody is meeting and simply doing it, without permission; he calls this ownership or championing. His central rule is that every gap in your hours and in the world will be filled with good or with evil, which is why evil rules and poor countries are bombed: people of good were too busy or embarrassed to raise their banner. The Prophet modelled this, keeping Quraysh permanently on the defensive despite having no numbers or wealth, and he supported initiatives like the seventy Qurra who worked by day, prayed by night and taught the people of Suffah trades. He then explains fard kifayah: the ummah has obligations no individual can fulfil alone, so those who step up, like the one who jumps in after a man overboard, are the heroes of a community. In the second khutbah he argues that one such deed, as with the people of Badr, Uthman and Musa, can outweigh a record of faults, lists neglected communal needs such as advocacy, dawah, mental health, riba-free finance and school curricula, and asks for a thousand Hudhuds.

outline.heading: Opening
Race to good deeds
outline.gist: Each person takes a direction in life, so take initiative and reach good as quickly as you can; wherever you are, Allah will bring you to judgment.

outline.heading: A contract between institution and attendee
outline.gist: The masjid has stated what it owes and will hold itself to it, but a population becomes a community only through a contract with those who attend. The Prophet set this in Makkah and twice with the Ansar before Madinah.

outline.heading: Attendance: the masjid as launching pad
outline.gist: In any city a Muslim looks for the masjid; it must be your reference point and launching pad. If people stop attending there is no point continuing the conversation.

outline.heading: Participation, and now initiative
outline.gist: Last week everyone was asked to participate in one of five domains. The third piece is initiative.

outline.heading: Syria's excuse, Canada's same lack
outline.gist: In 13 years here he has seen few initiatives. In Syria people blamed fear of the regime, but Muslims living freely in Canada take no more initiative.

outline.heading: Ideas are not initiatives
outline.gist: People bring him plenty of ideas for him to carry out. An initiative is noticing what needs doing and nobody is doing, and doing it yourself; Islam as a society is built so that you need no one's permission.

outline.heading: We need champions
outline.gist: Call it ownership or championing, as in his 2022 khutbah on champions: people who take up the missing links in society. Running a masjid and its programs is one initiative, but many more are needed.

outline.heading: Every void is filled with good or evil
outline.gist: Some pain simply comes with existence. Beyond that, every gap in the world and every empty hour in your life will be filled with good or with evil; there is no third option.

outline.heading: Why evil rules the world
outline.gist: Evil fills the voids that people of good left empty, which is why evil individuals govern and imperial powers bomb poor countries: Gaza, Sudan, Yemen, Myanmar, Iran, Iraq, Sham and beyond. People choose evil because few push back.

outline.heading: The banner of falsehood
outline.gist: A quote he values: the people of falsehood raised their banner and evil gathered around it, while the people of truth were too busy, distracted or embarrassed to raise theirs and stayed scattered.

outline.heading: Hasten to good deeds before the trials
outline.gist: The Prophet urged taking initiative with good before trials so heavy that a man sleeps a believer and wakes a disbeliever, selling his deen for a little worldly gain.

outline.heading: The Prophet kept Quraysh reacting
outline.gist: With none of their numbers, wealth, status or army, he was never on the ropes: he kept producing and Quraysh kept responding. For 200 years Muslims, despite huge numbers, have only reacted to what happens to them.

outline.heading: Whoever starts a good practice
outline.gist: Whoever starts a good practice in Islam earns its reward and that of all who follow. Initiatives run socially without needing the masjid; if we do not set good precedents, others set bad ones.

outline.heading: The seventy Qurra
outline.gist: Young men worked by day, prayed most of the night, studied Quran together and taught the poor of Suffah trades so they could make a living. When they were killed the Prophet prayed against their killers for a month.

outline.heading: Fard 'ayn and fard kifayah
outline.gist: Personal obligations fall on each individual; communal ones fall on the ummah as one organism. Since the whole ummah cannot do them, people must be chosen, or choose themselves, to carry them for everyone, and they are a community's heroes.

outline.heading: A man overboard
outline.gist: Not everyone on a boat can jump in after the man who fell, but if nobody does, all are accountable, and whoever does makes the headlines. No one thanks you for personal obligations; Allah will.

outline.heading: Endless problems swept under the rug
outline.gist: Taking initiative means fixing a problem we all suffer from but cannot all fix. The list is endless; ignored problems grow into monsters and we end up in damage control.

outline.heading: Interlude
Each of you stands at a frontier of Islam
outline.gist: Narrated weakly as a hadith but more correctly said by Umar during his caliphate: each of you guards an opening where Islam is vulnerable, so do not let it be breached through you.

outline.heading: One deed to point to when your book is read
outline.gist: When the book is read and full of things you would rather not read, you need one deed: a need you saw and gave your time, wealth and expertise to fill.

outline.heading: Yunus and Musa
outline.gist: Yunus left his people without permission and spent time in the whale. Musa seized Harun and threw down the tablets, yet the Quran never faults him, because he carried a weight no one else did.

outline.heading: Hatib and the people of Badr
outline.gist: When Umar called Hatib's letter betrayal, the Prophet answered that Allah may have looked at the people of Badr and forgiven them whatever they do, for the weight those 314 carried for everyone.

outline.heading: Nothing could harm Uthman after the army
outline.gist: Uthman equipped a whole army from his own wealth. Find the issue you will champion like that, without waiting to be assigned, asking permission or seeking praise.

outline.heading: Obligations no one is fulfilling
outline.gist: Carry some obligation on behalf of the ummah. Many communal obligations go unmet and all will be asked about them, except those trying to fulfil one.

outline.heading: Whose problems are these?
outline.gist: Advocacy, dawah, mental health, riba-free financing for cars and homes, school curricula: everyone knew these were problems. He challenges people to tell him whose responsibility they think they are.

outline.heading: It is all of our responsibility
outline.gist: The people you thought responsible carried their weight; are you carrying yours? Every community has quiet workers who focus on one thing for Allah without waiting for applause, and we need more.

outline.heading: The Hudhud
outline.gist: On an errand, the Hudhud noticed a kingdom worshipping the sun, investigated and came back late to Sulayman knowing he risked punishment. We need a thousand like him.

outline.heading: Evil loves voids
outline.gist: If everyone waits for someone else, nothing gets fixed. Evil positions itself in every void, so fill it with good first.

outline.heading: Outro

E5YRJR7xJ1Q.speaker_note: MWN Friday khutbah, second in his own 'Communal Covenant' series; refers to 13 years in the city and 'this place we call wellness'; a different voice speaks after the prayer from 41:54
E5YRJR7xJ1Q.title: Our Communal Covenant: Your End of the Bargain - Participation
E5YRJR7xJ1Q.one_line: The second communal commitment: participate with time, wealth and presence in one of five domains, because non-participation is the mark of hypocrites and dead weight.
E5YRJR7xJ1Q.summary: After restating that the Prophet never moved forward without a covenant with his community, he levels with an audience watching imperial powers bomb Gaza, Iran and Iraq: Muslims have no choice but to belong to the ummah and take a stance, but most of us lack the reach to stop anything now, so the work is for the long haul, building identity, knowledge and functioning institutions for the next generation. That begins with basics, first attendance and now participation. He grounds participation in 61:10-13, the transaction of believing and striving with wealth and lives, and in 3:166-167, where the hypocrites' defining trait at Uhud was refusing to show up. He shares an observation from Ramadan: when he asked seven hundred people to make dua for volunteers, fifty responded, and he traces the silence to disliking the setting, past embarrassment or being told to sit and follow. Participation matters because the young copy it; thirteen years of experience show that children whose parents attended with them stayed. Fundraising is a misnomer since you invest in your own community, and those who give nothing are dead weight, as at Tabuk. Be a participating, not a consuming, Muslim. In the second khutbah he names five domains, education, mentorship, financial centralization, outreach and advocacy, and asks everyone to pick one or two while staying balanced.

outline.heading: Opening
The covenant runs both ways
outline.gist: The Prophet never moved forward without an understanding with the companions, made in Makkah before Madinah, which is how the ummah achieved so much so fast. The first khutbah gave what masajid owe; now comes the community's end.

outline.heading: What we have watched since October 2023
outline.gist: Many young people began following the news then and have not been able to stop, as imperial powers bomb the birthplace of Islam out of hatred, racism, supremacy and arrogance.

outline.heading: No Muslim can opt out of the ummah
outline.gist: He agrees more should be done. Becoming Muslim means belonging to the Prophet's nation, so every Muslim must take a stance and participate somehow.

outline.heading: We lack the reach right now
outline.gist: Most of us do not have the status or influence to stop what is happening; we did not for two years of bombing in Gaza and its 60 to 70,000 dead, and we do not now for Iran and Iraq.

outline.heading: In it for the long haul
outline.gist: The question is how to build that reach. It took the Prophet 23 years and he did not live to see it flourish, so we must leave something of value for those who carry the baton.

outline.heading: Why showing up still matters
outline.gist: The next generation needs identity, knowledge and purposeful institutions. With no centralized leadership, the masjid is the only place Muslims can communicate and plan, and he cannot see how attending only at Eid and Jumuah keeps a family's Islam alive.

outline.heading: Point 2: participation, the transaction of As-Saff
outline.gist: After attendance comes participation. The verses offer a transaction: believe, then strive with your time, wealth and presence, and your sins are forgiven, Jannah is yours and your deeds open doors for those after you.

outline.heading: The most dangerous moment since 1943
outline.gist: The world has not been this close to wide danger since World War II. Muslims must still aim to establish justice, unity and a good state for the ummah.

outline.heading: Start with the basics: the child who wants to be a doctor
outline.gist: A grade one student reaches the goal by getting to grade three, then four, without losing sight of it. The ummah must keep its eye on dawah and justice while taking simple steps.

outline.heading: Not participating, the hypocrites' main sign
outline.gist: Start by agreeing on what places like this offer and what others do. Beyond their ethical signs, the main mark of the hypocrites was that they did not participate.

outline.heading: Uhud: fight, or at least stand with us
outline.gist: The hypocrites were asked to fight or simply swell the ranks to defend Madinah, and went home claiming there would be no battle; that day they were nearer to disbelief than faith.

outline.heading: Fifty voices out of seven hundred
outline.gist: In the last ten nights of Ramadan he asks people to make dua for the volunteers. Of six or seven hundred, perhaps fifty respond and the rest just stare.

outline.heading: Why people hold back
outline.gist: Disliking the masjid's direction, having been made self-conscious before, being told just to sit and follow, or feeling they do not belong are all wrong reasons. When he pushed, people grew offended, so he stopped and apologized.

outline.heading: The young learn from what adults do
outline.gist: When a son sees adults sit silent he concludes it is lame. The same holds for financial, political and social participation: if the older generation does not participate, the younger will not.

outline.heading: Children whose parents sat beside them stayed
outline.gist: Thirteen years in the city show that those still memorizing and attending as adults are the ones whose parents sat with them in lessons they did not need themselves.

outline.heading: Fundraising is the wrong word
outline.gist: He and the masjid do not need funds; the community does. Giving is not giving to someone else but investing in your own future and your children's.

outline.heading: Dead weight: the army against the Romans
outline.gist: Preparing an army to keep the Muslims from annihilation, the Prophet counted heads against wealth and half had given nothing. That dead weight pulls communities down; participation is the clear line between believer and hypocrite.

outline.heading: The participating Muslim and the consuming Muslim
outline.gist: Give more than you take. Do not be the Muslim who shows up only when he needs a service.

outline.heading: Interlude
Every Muslim picks one of five domains
outline.gist: He returns to the five domains of communal participation he set out years ago; everyone must choose one, more if very talented.

outline.heading: Domain 1: education
outline.gist: An educated community that knows its deen well, and is well informed beyond it, is the basis of the religion.

outline.heading: Domain 2: mentorship
outline.gist: A barrier between generations ruins identity. Youth need role models, and mentoring needs life experience, not information: be alive and still Muslim.

outline.heading: Domain 3: financial centralization
outline.gist: Pooling zakat and sadaqah is at least one form of unity, so wealth can be directed to the needy, to institutions and to projects such as outreach.

outline.heading: The same volunteers in every committee
outline.gist: Whenever he asks for volunteers it is the same people, each on fifteen committees, recycled in every institution while everyone else is absent.

outline.heading: Domain 4: locally brewed outreach
outline.gist: Dedicated groups must bring dawah to Muslims who do not come to the masjid and to non-Muslims, grounded in the struggles of Muslims in Canada, which differ from those elsewhere.

outline.heading: Domain 5: advocacy
outline.gist: Sudan is the world's worst humanitarian crisis yet is forgotten while bombing happens elsewhere. People are needed who win a seat at the table for Muslim values.

outline.heading: One or two at most, and stay balanced
outline.gist: Do not spread yourself thin or neglect family, health, wealth or career for communal work. The Prophet ran a family, kept friends and cared for himself while serving fully.

outline.heading: The poor who brought a few dates
outline.gist: Hypocrites mocked the poor who brought two or three dates or offered only their labour; Allah mocks the mockers, because everyone must shoulder some weight.

outline.heading: Interlude
Participation beyond the institution
outline.gist: Sometimes people must find ways to participate outside these walls. Community-driven work lasts longer and goes farther than work under an institution's umbrella, so collaborate.

outline.heading: Outro

pS7s29Utbgg.speaker_note: Sheikh Adnan reviews his own year of tazkiyah sessions and tells of his imprisonment in Syria and arrival in Canada
pS7s29Utbgg.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Review and Introduction to Self-Value
pS7s29Utbgg.one_line: A review of the framework of tazkiyah, why it protects Islam's ethics, then an introduction to self-value through the pendulum of vanity and inferiority.
pS7s29Utbgg.summary: The sheikh first reviews his tazkiyah framework: every Muslim needs a creed, a school of fiqh and a spiritual and ethical approach; tazkiyah has four categories (comprehension, connection, rituals, exercises), four daily focuses (the inner side of every act, servanthood, intention, acceptance of deeds) and four rules, chief of which is that everything taught applies to you, never to others. He answers how tazkiyah relates to the ethics series: knowing the moral algorithm takes a session, but without self-honesty people bend the truth until wrong feels right, which is why tyrants do not believe they are evil. Accepting mortality is the one truth all agree on. He then opens the pillar of self-value. Using his teacher's image of a two-storey pendulum, he shows vanity and low self-esteem, arrogance and inferiority as one swinging system; the healthy centre is confidence plus humility, which he calls tawadu'. Deriving worth from comparison, achievement or opinion makes worth a variable and life a misery. True value is divine and fixed: Allah honoured the children of Adam and only He knows taqwa. Emotions driven by the swing are pseudo-emotions, like a drug. He illustrates with his own loss of status after prison and emigration, and a teacher who served a guest imam for a week to cure a moment of envy.

outline.heading: Opening
Three requirements of every Muslim
outline.gist: A creed, a school of fiqh to follow and a spiritual and ethical orientation, which is what tazkiyah provides.

outline.heading: Four categories of tazkiyah
outline.gist: Comprehension, connection through dhikr, the inner side of rituals, and exercises; these sessions focus on comprehension.

outline.heading: Four daily focuses
outline.gist: Think daily about the inner essence of every act, that you are a servant, your intention, and whether your deeds are accepted, until it becomes second nature.

outline.heading: Rule one: it is about you
outline.gist: Never apply what you hear to someone else; he holds only students who ask to be held to these rules.

outline.heading: Rule two: daily dhikr
outline.gist: Without a daily minimum of remembrance at least twice a day, none of this is worthwhile.

outline.heading: Rule three: daily contemplation
outline.gist: Let concepts marinate and think deeply, as the Prophet did with everything he encountered.

outline.heading: Rule four: actually do the exercises
outline.gist: The discomfort an exercise brings is the point; find out why you resist it.

outline.heading: Principles and methods of change
outline.gist: Change is gradual, built on habits, self-honesty and replacing bad habits with good, through external and internal forces, lifestyle change and reinforcement.

outline.heading: Nothing original, organised for Canada
outline.gist: Everything he teaches is in the classical books, reordered with examples suited to North America, as he taught it differently in Syria.

outline.heading: Why people do not follow ethics they agree with
outline.gist: Most humans accept the same moral compass; tazkiyah protects your ability to apply the ethical algorithm and see truth as truth.

outline.heading: Self-honesty stops self-justification
outline.gist: To do wrong while valuing truth, you must convince yourself it is right; self-accountability guards against spinning the narrative.

outline.heading: Protecting Islam's moral constants
outline.gist: Morality is what Islam brings most uniquely; the Quran says testify for justice even against your parents, but in the moment people find a million excuses.

outline.heading: No one believes they are evil
outline.gist: Tyrants surround themselves with people who reinforce their lies until their conscience sleeps; some will even swear to Allah they were right.

outline.heading: Mortality: the one truth everyone accepts
outline.gist: Death is certain and sooner than we like; if you cannot accept that, there is no hope you will accept any other truth.

outline.heading: An expiry date on every organ
outline.gist: The body is not built to last; replacing every organ would simply be a new person, and tazkiyah is the pursuit of truth.

outline.heading: Self-value: the first pillar
outline.gist: He has spent about two and a half years on this pillar in his sessions because nothing else works without it.

outline.heading: Self-value is the truth about you
outline.gist: The truth about your worth is less attractive than the nafs's story but grounded; lies from yourself or your community cause lifelong grief.

outline.heading: Amr ibn Abasa: free men and slaves
outline.gist: Asked who followed the Prophet, the answer was a free man and a slave: a revolutionary narrative of equal human worth, not only an ethic.

outline.heading: Raised to prove our worth
outline.gist: From childhood, especially for boys, we are pushed to prove value, often through what we are affiliated with.

outline.heading: Value to a team versus value as a person
outline.gist: He is useful on an oncology team and a liability on a basketball team; domain value varies, absolute self-value should not.

outline.heading: The pendulum: vanity and low self-esteem
outline.gist: His teacher's image: a pendulum on a bumpy road swings between self-centred vanity and thinking little of yourself.

outline.heading: The lower storey: arrogance and inferiority
outline.gist: Vanity concerns how you see yourself, arrogance how you see others; both storeys swing together.

outline.heading: What swings one way swings back
outline.gist: The nafs pushes the pendulum toward superiority, but it cannot stay there, so vain people are the same people who suffer low self-esteem.

outline.heading: The centre: confidence plus humility
outline.gist: Self-confidence with humility toward others is tawadu', the master of all ethics.

outline.heading: Variables make your value a variable
outline.gist: If worth comes from comparisons or achievements, every win and loss swings the pendulum.

outline.heading: Animal instincts: lions and orcas
outline.gist: Rival lions kill each other's cubs and defeated males die alone; the nafs carries the same drive for dominance from the earth.

outline.heading: Nafs and ruh; questions to contemplate
outline.gist: The nafs mirrors the ethics of the soil, the spirit those of God; should the pendulum swing at all, and where do you get your value?

outline.heading: If my value is your opinion of me
outline.gist: Am I less when you think less of me? Value from people, achievements or comparison is always unstable.

outline.heading: Your value is divine and fixed
outline.gist: Nothing makes you more or less human; Allah honoured the children of Adam, so no one can add to or subtract from your worth.

outline.heading: Nothing to prove, and no one is above you
outline.gist: Prison or ruined reputation cannot touch it, nor can reverence raise it; the most honoured are the most pious, which only Allah can measure.

outline.heading: Domain value is not human value
outline.gist: A doctor or scholar is more valuable in their field, not as a person; confusing the two guarantees misery.

outline.heading: The endless swing is hell
outline.gist: Attach your worth to changing sources and you will never feel at peace; Islam cuts those wires and holds the pendulum still.

outline.heading: Children raised secure in their worth
outline.gist: He has seen children of wealthy non-Muslim families who are not threatened by others' opinions, which we dismiss as entitlement.

outline.heading: Families that teach you to keep proving
outline.gist: Many immigrant families raise children to earn their worth, so every achievement brings a brief high and then emptiness.

outline.heading: How will I motivate myself?
outline.gist: That proving worth is the only motivation people know is itself a sad sign; motivation must come from elsewhere.

outline.heading: Secure but unmotivated: half the equation
outline.gist: Children given value but no reason to strive become idle; those driven by feeling less achieve without meaning.

outline.heading: Famous athletes who collapse after retiring
outline.gist: Decades of worth from adulation swing back violently once it ends.

outline.heading: Pseudo-emotions like a drug
outline.gist: Feelings driven by the swing are addictive and false; real emotion feels dull at first, like life after cocaine.

outline.heading: Why salah feels empty
outline.gist: Salah offers no swing, so people feel nothing until the imam moves them; the companions wept in prayer because the Prophet freed them from this.

outline.heading: Learn to tell real joy from a boost
outline.gist: Start separating genuine happiness from feelings of being better or worse, and cut the wires.

outline.heading: Prison, exile and starting from nothing
outline.gist: He thought he had mastered this until he was jailed in Syria and then arrived in Canada no longer a physician or sheikh, and found he still drew some value from status.

outline.heading: His teacher who served the guest imam
outline.gist: Feeling a flicker of envy when a friend outshone him, his teacher kept the guest for a week and served him to purge it.

outline.heading: Achievements mean nothing to your value
outline.gist: The nafs plugs in a new wire the moment you look away; if you understand Allah, accomplishments add nothing to who you are.

outline.heading: Losing everything as a blessing
outline.gist: Running a masjid and practising medicine had made him dependent; being stripped of it taught him what knowing alone could not.

outline.heading: Deeds do not change your value; religiosity is the worst source
outline.gist: Good deeds bring you closer to Allah but do not make you more human; feeling worth from piety is a trap, so find another motive for repentance.

outline.heading: Loose ends to think about
outline.gist: He leaves questions open deliberately for contemplation before the next session.

outline.heading: Outro
